node.label: Nancy Fraser
node.date_label: Unruly Practices (1989) · “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) · Tanner Lectures on redistribution and recognition (1996) · “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014)
node.description: A philosopher and critical theorist who reworked Habermas’s public sphere and the theory of justice from a feminist standpoint. In “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) she criticised the liberal model of the bourgeois public sphere that Habermas had described, for discounting the effects of social inequality and for its masculinist bias, and argued for a plurality of contesting publics, including what she called subaltern counterpublics. Jane Mansbridge (2017) credits the essay with moves that became established in deliberative democracy, from Habermas’s unitary public to Fraser’s plural publics. In “From Redistribution to Recognition?” (1995), expanded in her Tanner Lectures (1996) and collected in Justice Interruptus (1997), she argued that justice requires both redistribution and recognition; the lectures treat gender as a “bivalent collectivity” and propose participatory parity as the norm of justice; she rejected Charles Taylor’s and Axel Honneth’s grounding of recognition in self-realization. Judith Butler’s “Merely Cultural” (1997) prompted Fraser’s published reply, which rejected the suggestion that she treated heterosexism as merely cultural, and Redistribution or Recognition? staged a sustained debate with Honneth. With the historian Linda Gordon she co-wrote “A Genealogy of Dependency” (1994), on a keyword of the US welfare state. In “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014) she looks behind Marx’s “hidden abode” of production for the conditions it depends on, reworking his account from feminist, ecological and political perspectives, and “Contradictions of Capital and Care” (2016) argues that every form of capitalist society harbours a social-reproductive contradiction.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Foucault on Modern Power” (1981); “What’s Critical about Critical Theory? The Case of Habermas and Gender” (1985); Unruly Practices: Power, Discourse, and Gender in Contemporary Social Theory (1989); “Rethinking the Public Sphere: A Contribution to the Critique of Actually Existing Democracy” (1990); “A Genealogy of Dependency” (1994, with Linda Gordon); “Social Justice in the Age of Identity Politics” (Tanner Lectures, 1996); “Heterosexism, Misrecognition, and Capitalism: A Response to Judith Butler” (1997); Redistribution or Recognition? (2003, with Axel Honneth); “Transnationalizing the Public Sphere” (2007); “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014); “Contradictions of Capital and Care” (2016); Cannibal Capitalism (2022).
node.scope_note: The Tanner lecture text (1996) and “Transnationalizing the Public Sphere” (2007) were read in full on open routes. Only the openly visible openings of the New Left Review essays (1998, 2014, 2016) were read. “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) was not read for this draft: its argument is described from Fraser’s own 2007 summary and from Mansbridge’s abstract. Unruly Practices and Redistribution or Recognition? are described from publisher pages only. The Fraser–Gordon articles are known from Gordon’s CV and Crossref; their texts are unread. Cannibal Capitalism is listed by title only, and its year comes from the citation record.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990), as she summarised it in 2007, Fraser criticised what she called, following Habermas, the liberal model of the bourgeois public sphere, for discounting the effects of social inequality on public opinion and for its masculinist bias, while keeping the public sphere as a concept to be reconstructed; in “Transnationalizing the Public Sphere” (2007) she argued that Habermas’s account tacitly assumed a Westphalian, nation-state frame.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Transversal text (2007), section “Classical Public Sphere Theory and Its Radical Critique”: Habermas’s Structural Transformation as “the locus classicus of all discussions”; her own earlier article “directed criticisms of both types against … the liberal model of the bourgeois public sphere”; the legitimacy critique “focused on the effects on public opinion of inequality within civil society”, “Exposing, too, the bourgeois masculinist bias”; “Tacitly, however, Habermas's account of the public sphere rested on at least six social-theoretical presuppositions”. Introduction: public sphere theory is a resource that “should be reconstructed rather than jettisoned”. Mansbridge’s abstract (2017) independently describes the move “from Habermas's unitary conception to Fraser's plurality of contesting publics”. Limits: Fraser dates her earlier article 1991 in this text; the Social Text printing is 1990 (Crossref 10.2307/466240). The 1990 article itself was not read on a permitted route for this draft (JSTOR did not load). Distinct from existing edges gender → jurgen_habermas (edge_652, edge_1511), which describe Fraser’s critique but have no Fraser endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Heterosexism, Misrecognition, and Capitalism: A Response to Judith Butler” (Social Text, 1997; New Left Review, 1998), Fraser welcomed Butler’s “Merely Cultural” but disputed its account of Marxism’s legacy, of poststructuralism and of contemporary capitalism, and rejected the suggestion that she treated heterosexist oppression as merely cultural.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NLR I/228 page, visible opening: “Judith Butler's essay is welcome on several counts”; “Nevertheless, Butler and I disagree”; disagreement over the legacy of Marxism, the assessment of poststructuralism and the character of contemporary capitalism; objection that Butler’s use of the “neoconservative Marxist” critique to frame Justice Interruptus is “unfortunate” because it could suggest Fraser treats heterosexism as “merely cultural”. Remainder paywalled, unread. Original Social Text 52/53 (1997) printing from Crossref metadata only. The Tanner text (1996 lectures as published) cites “Merely Cultural” as “the counterargument” (p. 21 n. 21). Butler’s own visible preview names no target, so no reverse edge is drawn; the coordinator may make this one undirected as an exchange if a Butler passage naming Fraser is later read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fraser and the historian Linda Gordon co-wrote “A Genealogy of Dependency: Tracing a Keyword of the U.S. Welfare State” (Signs, 1994) and “Civil Citizenship against Social Citizenship? On the Ideology of Contract-versus-Charity” (1994).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gordon’s own CV, publications list: “A Genealogy of ‘Dependency’: Tracing a Keyword of the US Welfare State,” with Nancy Fraser, Signs, winter 1994, “and in many anthologies”; “Civil Citizenship Against Social Citizenship? …,” with Nancy Fraser, in van Steenbergen, ed., The Condition of Citizenship (CV: “The Quality of Citizenship”), 1994. Crossref DOI 10.1086/494886: Fraser and Gordon, Signs 19, no. 2 (1994): 309–336. Co-authorship of substantive articles only; the article text and its argument are unread (publisher 403, JSTOR did not load), so no claim about content is made.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her Tanner Lectures (1996), Fraser presented Taylor as a leading proponent of the politics of recognition but rejected his treatment of recognition as a matter of self-realization grounded in a thick theory of the good, arguing instead that recognition is a matter of justice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tanner lecture text: p. 10, “proponents of the politics of recognition, such as Charles Taylor, insist that” a difference-blind politics of redistribution can reinforce injustice (n. 10 cites “The Politics of Recognition”); p. 24, “two major theorists, Charles Taylor and Axel Honneth, understand recognition as a matter of self-realization”, and she rejects justifying claims “by reference to a thick theory of the good, as Taylor does” (n. 23 cites “The Politics of Recognition” and Sources of the Self); p. 34 with n. 36. Body-text engagement. Page numbers from partly garbled running headers. Honneth (also criticised, pp. 24, 27, 29) is not an endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014), Fraser takes Marx’s move from exchange into the “hidden abode” of production as her starting point and proposes to look further behind it, to the conditions of possibility of production.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NLR 86 page, visible opening: “While Marx looked behind the sphere of exchange, into the ‘hidden abode’ of production”; “I shall seek production's conditions of possibility behind that sphere, in realms that are more hidden still”; she describes reconstructing his insights through feminist, ecological and political perspectives. A stated building-on and extension of Marx, not adoption of all his claims. Rest of essay paywalled, unread. The Tanner text also cites Marx for the Marxian concept of class (p. 8 n. 7), not used here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her Tanner Lectures (1996), Fraser models the collectivities of the politics of recognition on Weber’s status groups, defined by esteem and prestige rather than by relation to production, citing his “Class, Status, Party”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tanner lecture text, p. 8: in the recognition paradigm “the victims of injustice are more like Weberian status groups than Marxian (or Weberian) classes”; n. 8: “For the Weberian definition of class, see Max Weber, ‘Class, Status, Party’”; p. 31 n. 31 notes that “Weber's own distinction was tripartite not bipartite”. A conceptual borrowing named in the body text; no broader debt to Weber claimed. Flag for reviewers as a moderate-strength edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Mascaretti reconstructs her critique, Fraser’s “Foucault on Modern Power: Empirical Insights and Normative Confusions” (1981; collected in Unruly Practices, 1989) questions the normative basis of Foucault’s analyses of power; “Michel Foucault: A ‘Young Conservative’?” (1985) asks why a fully panopticized society should be opposed.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Giovanni Maria Mascaretti, “Foucault, Normativity, and Freedom: A Reappraisal” (2019), https://rauli.cbs.dk/index.php/foucault-studies/article/download/5890/6560/21348, section 1, pp. 25–26 and notes 7–12. Mediated interpretation explicitly attributed in the sentence; Fraser’s original essays remain unread. Her own bibliography at https://nancyfrasernet.wordpress.com/publications/, first and fourth entries, confirms the original years. The 1985 journal record is https://doi.org/10.1086/292729. Existing nf_n_umn_unruly remains bibliographic context; the substantive witness is Mascaretti, identified here by full citation and URL.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fraser reconstructs critical theory from a feminist standpoint: Unruly Practices (1989) proposes a socialist-feminist critical theory built on the politics of need interpretation, and “Rethinking the Public Sphere” (1990) brought the term “subaltern counterpublics” into critical theoretical discourse.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: University of Minnesota Press page: “Nancy Fraser develops a new and original socialist-feminist critical theory”; “the politics of need interpretation” as its “linchpin”. Mansbridge abstract (2017): the essay “brought the term ‘subaltern counterpublics’ into critical theoretical discourse”. Transversal (2007): public sphere theory is “an important critical-conceptual resource that should be reconstructed rather than jettisoned”. Fraser already has a frankfurt roster row (role critic) resting on fraser_sphere_primary; this is the first edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her Tanner Lectures (1996), Fraser argued that gender is a “bivalent collectivity” with both a political-economic and a cultural face, so that gender injustice requires both redistribution and recognition; her public-sphere critique had earlier exposed the masculinist bias in liberal views of what counts as a public concern.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tanner lecture text: p. 15, “Gender, I contend, is a bivalent collectivity”, encompassing “both political-economic dimensions and cultural-valuational dimensions”; “Understanding and redressing gender injustice requires attending to both distribution and recognition”; p. 17, “Gender, in sum, is a bivalent mode of collectivity”; p. 18, “Gender, we can now see, explodes this whole series of false antitheses.” Transversal (2007), her own summary of the 1990/1991 critique: “Exposing, too, the bourgeois masculinist bias in standard liberal views of what counts as a public concern”. A theoretical contribution to the analysis of gender, not historical research of her own. Distinct from existing edges gender → jurgen_habermas.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Subjects of Empire? (2009), Glen Coulthard criticises Fraser’s status model in Redistribution or Recognition? (2003) for insufficiently addressing the psychological dimensions of misrecognition, arguing that removing structural obstacles to participatory parity may leave those dimensions of domination intact.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the repository dissertation’s printed pp. 52–57. Coulthard acknowledges the institutional model’s advantages but argues, through Fanon, that psychological injuries can persist independently. Specific critique only; Fraser’s 2003 book was not independently read here. Only scholarly argument is represented.
proposed_edges.map_label: Critiques the status model of recognition

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Behind Marx’s Hidden Abode” (2014), Fraser contributes to political economy by proposing to reconstruct the analysis of capitalism around gender, ecology and political power as well as production.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s visible opening through its initial account of capital accumulation. Fraser explicitly asks how capitalism should be conceptualized and proposes reconstructing inherited theory through these additional dimensions. The claim records this stated intervention only; the remainder requires subscription and was not read. Political economy is the existing economictheory endpoint; this does not assert that Fraser founded a field.
